# 0010: Per-pod, in-memory rate limit

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-19
- **Modules:** upload-service
- **Source:** design doc, section "Where the rate limit is counted" (linked from README.md in this folder)

## Decision

Count uploads per MAC in each pod's memory, default 30 per 10 minutes, behind a `RateLimiter` interface. A shared
implementation can replace it later without touching callers.

## Rules for agents

Callers use the `RateLimiter` interface only; don't add a network call (Redis, Valkey) to the upload path without a new record.

9	| Daily volume | 11.67 M PUTs and 2.38 M HEADs a day (HEAD only before app.log). By type: calls.xml 65%, app.log 21%, core dumps 13%, then phone.cfg 57 k and boot.log 30 k. | Confirms about 11 M a day. calls.xml is most of the load, so storing or rejecting it is a real decision (ADR 0008). |
10	| Peak rate | 135/s daily average. Peak hour 15:00 to 16:00 UTC at 272/s; busiest second 532/s. Quietest hour about 46/s. | About twice the brief's 127/s. Replicas and load tests sized for at least 550/s (`docs/load-tests/`). |
11	| Phones and per-MAC rate | About 600 k phones a day upload app.log and 359 k upload calls.xml. PUTs per MAC in 10 minutes: median 1, p99 6, max 114. One MAC went over 30. | A limit of 30 per 10 minutes is safe for normal phones and catches the outlier (ADR 0010). |
12	| Retries today, after 405 | app.log repeats about every 64 s; calls.xml at 60, 120 or 300 s; core dumps in quick bursts. 66 k distinct core files were sent 1.52 M times (about 23 each), some dated 2018. | Expect a burst of about 66 k old core dumps once the service answers 200, then normal volume. In the load-test profile. |
13	| Status codes today | 99.98% of PUTs get 405. Also 408 (about 2.6 k a day), 400 (721), 413 (187, mostly core dumps) and 500 (15). | Some core dumps are very large, possibly over 1 GiB (unverified), which drives the size limits and the timeout headroom (ADR 0005). |

# Production upload volumes, measured 2026-10-15

One full day of pccfg access logs in OCI Log Analytics (`VO_Phone_SSL_log`, us-phoenix-1, Thursday 2026-10-15, UTC).
Read-only queries on 2026-10-16, with MACs and file names masked. One weekday in one region. OCI keeps 5 to 7 days,
so these numbers cannot be re-measured; they are kept here because several decisions rest on them.

| Finding | Result | What it changed |
|---|---|---|
| Daily volume | 11.67 M PUTs and 2.38 M HEADs a day (HEAD only before app.log). By type: calls.xml 65%, app.log 21%, core dumps 13%, then phone.cfg 57 k and boot.log 30 k. | Confirms about 11 M a day. calls.xml is most of the load, so storing or rejecting it is a real decision (ADR 0008). |
| Peak rate | 135/s daily average. Peak hour 15:00 to 16:00 UTC at 272/s; busiest second 532/s. Quietest hour about 46/s. | About twice the brief's 127/s. Replicas and load tests sized for at least 550/s (`docs/load-tests/`). |
| Phones and per-MAC rate | About 600 k phones a day upload app.log and 359 k upload calls.xml. PUTs per MAC in 10 minutes: median 1, p99 6, max 114. One MAC went over 30. | A limit of 30 per 10 minutes is safe for normal phones and catches the outlier (ADR 0010). |
| Retries today, after 405 | app.log repeats about every 64 s; calls.xml at 60, 120 or 300 s; core dumps in quick bursts. 66 k distinct core files were sent 1.52 M times (about 23 each), some dated 2018. | Expect a burst of about 66 k old core dumps once the service answers 200, then normal volume. In the load-test profile. |
| Status codes today | 99.98% of PUTs get 405. Also 408 (about 2.6 k a day), 400 (721), 413 (187, mostly core dumps) and 500 (15). | Some core dumps are very large, possibly over 1 GiB (unverified), which drives the size limits and the timeout headroom (ADR 0005). |
| File names seen | `<MAC>-app.log`, `calls.xml`, `boot.log`, `audit.log`, `plcmsyslog.tar.gz`, `phone.cfg`, `web.cfg`; core dumps in three layouts (`enc.` and `enc1.`); crash logs (`apanic_console`, `dmesg-ramoops`). No `-now-` names. About 54 bad paths per 10 minutes from bad log-directory settings. | The file-name rules must cover these or reject them on purpose (ADR 0007). |
| Phone models | VVX 75%, Edge E 25%, Trio 0.4%, CCX 0.3%. Nearly all uploads come from the Application stage, not the Updater. | Lab tests cover VVX and Edge E first. |
| TLS versions | Not measurable: the request log that records the TLS version is not sent to OCI. | Confirmed in the lab instead (TLS 1.2 only). |

# 0009: Specific status codes, require Content-Length, never 503

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Modules:** upload-service, local
- **Source:** design doc, section "Status codes and Content-Length" (linked from README.md in this folder)

## Decision

Answer with specific codes and require Content-Length. Requiring a length lets the service stream with no buffering and
reject large files before reading them. Phones do not retry 429 and lose nothing: `app.log` carries its lines into the
next upload and the other files are full copies every time.

The codes: 400 for a bad name or a body that ends before Content-Length, 403 for a disabled type or an identity
problem, 408 for a body that stops arriving, 411 with no length, 413 when too large, 429 for the rate limit, a key
collision and storage failures. Tomcat sends the 400 and 408 for a broken body itself; the service records the same code
so the log line matches what the phone got.

## Rules for agents

Never return 503, and never read the body before every check has passed.

/**
 * RateLimiter: the interface the upload flow asks "may this MAC upload now?".
 *
 * Will define one operation that takes a MAC and answers allowed or limited.
 *
 * How it contributes: callers never know where the count lives, so a shared Redis/Valkey
 * limiter can replace the in-memory one later without touching them.
 */

content.text:
**Is it safe?** Yes, according to the one measurement the repo has. It is a single weekday in one region (us-phoenix-1, 2026-10-15), and it can't be re-measured because OCI keeps logs for only 5 to 7 days.

**The measurement:** PUTs per MAC in 10 minutes had a median of 1, a p99 of 6 and a max of 114. Only one MAC went over 30. The research note concludes that 30 per 10 minutes "is safe for normal phones and catches the outlier." ADR 0010 sets that as the default.

**Status for an over-limit phone:** 429 (ADR 0009). Phones don't retry on 429 and lose nothing, because `app.log` carries its lines into the next upload and the other files are full copies each time. The service never returns 503. But the limiter isn't wired in yet: `RateLimiter` and `InMemoryRateLimiter` exist, but policy doesn't call them, and `openapi.yaml` still says "Still to add: 429 for the rate limit." So today an over-limit phone isn't limited at all.

**Shared counter:** The design allows for one, but not without a new decision. ADR 0010 puts the per-pod in-memory count behind the `RateLimiter` interface so that a shared Redis/Valkey version "can replace it later without touching callers." However, its rule says not to add a network call to the upload path without a new ADR that supersedes 0010. Redis or Valkey would also be a new dependency, which needs a person's approval first. So the code is ready for the swap, but someone has to make the decision first.
